item.title: How Sleep Affects Metabolism and Weight
item.description:
Sleep

How Sleep Affects Metabolism and Weight

New research links sleep to growth hormone, activity, and weight.

Posted July 19, 2026

Key points
  • Sleep actively regulates hormones, metabolism, recovery, and next-day activity.
  • Losing about 80 minutes of sleep nightly was linked to modest weight gain.
  • Short sleep may increase sedentary behavior, not just hunger and cravings.
  • Sleep supports metabolic health but is not a stand-alone weight-loss treatment.
Source: daha3131053 / Pixabay

We often treat sleep as time taken away from more productive or enjoyable activities. We stay up to finish work, answer emails, watch another episode, or reclaim a little personal time at the end of the day.

The usual assumption is that the main consequence will be feeling tired the next morning. But two recent studies suggest that sleep loss may affect much more than alertness. Sleep is an active biological process that helps regulate hormones, metabolism, physical restoration, and how much we move the following day.

One study identified a brain circuit connecting sleep with growth hormone release. The other found that losing only about 80 minutes of sleep per night for six weeks was associated with modest weight gain and increased sedentary behavior.

Together, the findings suggest that regularly cutting sleep short may subtly shift the body toward poorer metabolic health, even when the sleep loss does not seem severe.

What the Brain Does During Sleep

Growth hormone is often associated with childhood development or athletic performance, but it remains important throughout adulthood. It contributes to tissue repair, muscle and bone maintenance, fat metabolism, and glucose regulation.

Scientists have long known that growth hormone secretion is closely tied to sleep, especially deep non-REM sleep. What has been less clear is how the brain coordinates that relationship.

In a study published in Cell, researchers examined neurons in the hypothalamus, a brain region involved in sleep, appetite, body temperature, and hormone regulation. Working with mice, they identified interactions between neurons that release growth hormone–releasing hormone, or GHRH, and neurons that produce somatostatin, which generally inhibits growth hormone secretion.

The researchers also found that growth hormone sends information back to the brain. After being released during sleep, it influenced activity in the locus coeruleus, a brainstem region involved in wakefulness, attention, and arousal.

This suggests that sleep and growth hormone operate through a feedback loop. Sleep helps stimulate growth hormone release, while the hormone may help regulate the brain’s eventual transition back toward wakefulness.

The finding offers a possible biological explanation for something many people experience: Poor sleep does not only make us sleepy. It can leave us feeling physically depleted, mentally foggy, and insufficiently restored.

What Happens When People Sleep Less?

The second study examined the effects of modest sleep loss in humans.

Researchers pooled data from randomized crossover trials involving 95 adults who normally slept approximately seven to eight hours per night. During one six-week period, participants followed their usual sleep schedules. During another, they delayed bedtime by 90 minutes while maintaining their normal wake time.

The actual reduction in sleep averaged about 80 minutes per night. This is much closer to ordinary sleep loss than studies in which participants are limited to only four hours of sleep.

After six weeks of shortened sleep, participants had gained an average of approximately one pound. They also spent about 17 additional minutes per day being sedentary. The increase in sedentary time was greater among men and postmenopausal women, although the study was not large enough to establish definitive subgroup differences.

One pound may not sound dramatic. The study also does not mean that everyone who loses 80 minutes of sleep will gain a predictable amount of weight. It involved a relatively small number of participants and lasted only six weeks.

Still, the findings are notable because the sleep restriction was modest. Participants were not kept awake all night. They did something millions of people routinely do: They went to bed later while continuing to wake up at the same time.

Source: TyliJura / Pixabay

Sleep Loss May Reduce Movement

Discussions about sleep and weight usually focus on hunger. Short sleep can affect appetite hormones, food choices, impulse control, and the appeal of calorie-dense foods.

The human study points to another pathway: When people sleep less, they may also move less.

Being awake for more hours does not necessarily mean being active for more hours. Even after accounting for the additional waking time, researchers found that participants were more sedentary during the sleep-restriction period.

This makes intuitive sense. A tired person may skip exercise, take fewer steps, remain seated during breaks, or lack the energy for ordinary movement that normally occurs without much thought.

Sleep loss may therefore affect metabolism through several small, overlapping mechanisms: reduced restorative hormonal activity, greater fatigue, more sedentary behavior, changes in appetite, poorer food choices, and impaired glucose regulation.

None of these changes needs to be dramatic. Repeated over weeks or months, small shifts may accumulate.

Sleep Is Not a Weight-Loss Cure

These findings should not be reduced to the simplistic message that sleeping more guarantees weight loss.

Body weight is influenced by genetics, medications, medical and psychiatric conditions, stress, activity, food access, socioeconomic circumstances, and many other factors. Some people cannot extend their sleep simply by deciding to go to bed earlier.

Shift work, caregiving, insomnia, chronic pain, sleep apnea, anxiety, depression, and mania can all interfere with sleep. For these individuals, advice to “prioritize sleep” may be unrealistic or even frustrating.

The research also does not prove that increasing sleep will reverse weight gain. The human study examined what happened when people who normally obtained adequate sleep were asked to sleep less. It did not test sleep extension as a treatment for obesity.

The more reasonable conclusion is that sleep should be considered alongside nutrition and physical activity as part of metabolic health. It is not a replacement for either, but it helps shape the biological environment in which both operate.

Protecting Sleep Without Making It Another Chore

A useful first step may be identifying where sleep is being lost.

Is bedtime gradually drifting later? Are work demands extending into the evening? Is late-night screen use delaying sleep? Is alcohol, caffeine, medication, pain, mood instability, or a breathing problem interfering?

A consistent wake time, a darker and cooler bedroom, reduced late-night light exposure, and a brief wind-down routine may help. Persistent insomnia, loud snoring, gasping during sleep, severe daytime sleepiness, or major changes in sleep need deserve medical attention.

The lesson is not that one bad night will damage your metabolism. The concern is the repeated pattern in which mild sleep deprivation becomes normal and its effects become difficult to notice.

Sleep may look passive from the outside. Inside the brain and body, however, it is part of the machinery that regulates hormones, restores tissue, supports alertness, and prepares us to move through the next day.

When we repeatedly borrow time from sleep, the body may eventually collect the debt.

item.title: Why Your Adult Child Left and Stays Quiet Instead of Talking
item.description:
Parenting

Why Your Adult Child Left and Stays Quiet Instead of Talking

Estrangement isn't the result of a single moment. It festers for a long time.

Posted July 19, 2026

Key points
  • The hurt is not the trigger, the replay is.
  • Avoidance is not restraint. It is a missing skill.
  • A grievance never constructively discussed is a grievance that does not get tested.

From my experience counseling and coaching parents and adult children, the adult children who go "no contract" rarely do it over one fight or argument. They leave due to negative thought loops that replay a skewed perception of family history. They also lack the ability to have calm, constructive conversations with their parents. And to be fair, many parents also lack those skills, or if they have them, their own defenses as parents undermine them.

Parents often come to me feeling devastated. They are convinced there is an offense or a series of offenses that they must pay for. For sure, like most parents, they made some mistakes. But often there is not one, not a single one, to truly explain a cut-off, especially an abrupt cut-off. What I see instead is a different mechanism entirely. An adult child who never developed the skills to sit with a hurt, to name it out loud, and to work through it with the person who caused it. So instead, they perseverate. They do this alone for years until a private replay thought loop becomes a maddening verdict. The names in the examples below have been changed to protect confidentiality.

Both Alyson and Rick Can't Let It Go and Move On

Alyson looks great on the outside. At age thirty-one, she holds a job as a data analyst for a large pharmaceutical company. She has a fiancé and a few friends. Her father, Mark, and her mother divorced when she was thirteen. Mark was devastated by the divorce, but started dating sooner than anyone expected. He met a few relationship partners over the next few years and then remarried. Most people would say Mark did a decent job being involved with Alyson and was supportive of her over the years. Yet, Alyson can't let go of old slights she never discussed with Mark. She also perseverates on the belief, "My dad can't handle being alone."

Now, let's briefly look at Rick. He holds a lot of resentment toward his mother, Diane, who made a comment at Rick's college graduation. She can barely remember what the comment was at the time. But Rick kept replying to that comment for over a decade, layering all his other frustrations right on top of it. He did not think "it was worth it" to attempt a calm, constructive conversation with Diane.

Instead, his hurt calcified into an overarching narrative of "My mom never really saw who I am." Even though Rick's hurt had some kernels of truth, Diane felt that his choice to estrange himself from her was over the top. For Rick, whom I spoke with, he felt that avoidance was easier and safer than confrontation. So, his hurt stayed private, unprocessed, and in a perfectly locked position to fester. He erroneously convinced himself that distance was the only way to gain relief.

Overthinking Drives the Distancing

In both the cases of Alyson and Rick, let me be clear that they both had genuine pain and hurt. But unfortunately, neither was taught — in a culture that values cutting off parents as self-care —how to bring a grievance to its source instead of letting it metastasize. Resilience isn't the absence of hurt. Rather, it is the ability to sit with it long enough to work it through, rather than just "build a case."

This is the exact mechanism I discuss in my book, When Overthinking Overtakes Your Child, which further explains how negative, perseverative thought loops can impact children of all ages and stop them from taking constructive steps forward. In essence, it feels safer to avoid these thought loops than to face the challenges they pose. In the cases we are discussing here, that means not being able to go to their parents and say, "I'm feeling hurt and would like to clear the air." Sadly, by the time a grievance finally surfaces, it is not a fresh topic but a retreaded, fixed, amplified, rigid, negative belief that was not challenged by reality.

The Takeaway

If your adult child has gone radio silent, the most useful question may not be, "What did I do to cause this?" Rather, the better question is, "Did anyone teach them how to tell me when they feel hurt?" The honest answer is likely "No." So, gently reaching out with the goal of listening as the top priority may be the best place to start. You can lead with, "Would you agree that a calm, constructive conversation, where I commit to understanding you, could be a healthier option for both of us?" Be patient after you ask, and don't be attached to the results. There is a good chance you will eventually be pleasantly surprised.

item.title: Love and the Tragic Substitution of Power for Value
item.description:
Relationships

Love and the Tragic Substitution of Power for Value

Love is about value, not power.

Posted July 19, 2026

Key points
  • In love relationships, power struggles are not really about power — who gets to rule.
  • Most discord in love relationships rises from attempts to substitute power for value.
  • We cannot criticize, stonewall, nag, manipulate, coerce, or threaten someone into loving us.
  • Empowerment is confidence to be vulnerable and regulate disappointment when partners are unreceptive.

In love relationships, power struggles are not essentially about power – who gets to rule. They’re about value, specifically, attempts to compensate for precipitous drops in self-value. When self-value falls, as it typically does in arguments with loved ones, partners feel vulnerable but unsafe to expose their vulnerability. To feel less vulnerable, they try to exert power over their partners, either overtly, through devaluing language, or covertly, through sarcasm, tone of voice, body language, and facial expressions.

These are the mindsets of power struggles in love relationships:

  • Being right at all costs
  • Winning (getting what you want)
  • Punishing (pouting, withdrawal of affection)
  • Diagnosing (something is mentally wrong with my partner)
  • Looking for things to resent

These were not the mindsets of falling in love. No one falling in love has fantasies of power: "I'm going to make this sucker do whatever I want!"

We fall in love with fantasies of value, of loving and being loved. Yet most discord in love relationships results from substituting power for value.

The exertion of power in love sometimes gets compliance (your lover relents and does what you want), sometimes fear, always resentment, but never value. You cannot criticize, stonewall, nag, manipulate, coerce, or threaten someone into genuinely valuing you. More importantly, you cannot feel valuable while exerting power over loved ones.

Couples in power struggles act as if they can change the negative impressions partners have of them by:

  • Arguing
  • Contradicting
  • “Reasoning”
  • Ridiculing
  • Devaluing

None of the above improves negative impressions held by partners, who feel betrayed when there is no understanding and compassion in their loved ones’ behavior.

One principle of emotional interaction improves relationships. The other dooms them to power struggles.

The first is positive reciprocity. If you approach a loved one with positive emotions (interest, enjoyment, curiosity, compassion, kindness, or affection), you typically get a positive response. (When you don’t get a positive response, factors outside the interaction predominate — loss, physical discomfort, anxiety, or sleep deprivation, etc.)

The second principle of emotional interaction is negative reactivity. Approaching a human (or animal) with negative emotions will garner a negative response nearly 100% of the time. Negative emotions are more contagious and get priority processing in the brain, which is why power struggles in love relationships are likely to end in frustration and exhaustion.

Finally, the condemning emotions — anger, resentment, contempt — feel different on the inside from the way they look on the outside. On the inside, it feels like you’re treated unfairly or disrespectfully; on the outside, you seem unfair and disrespectful, if not mean. Anger evolved in all animals as a response to perceived threats. It makes us warn, threaten, intimidate, or harm. This is what our bodies are visibly prepared to do, even though we might think that we merely want to make a point.

The Exquisite Vulnerability of Love

Power struggles occur when we try to avoid the vulnerability necessary for intimate relationships to thrive. Fear of exposing vulnerability implies that our partners will not love us if we show our whole self. The only way to be sure of our partners’ love is to expose vulnerability and see that our partners still love us.

Empowerment in love is the confidence to expose vulnerability and regulate disappointment when our partners are in unreceptive states.

The most reliable way to free relationships from the grip of power struggles is for each partner to regulate self-value internally, so it is never at stake and can never diminish in interactions. You are just as valuable, regardless of whether you get what you want. Core value does not depend on validation by others. Rather, it’s supported by your own humane values (including compassion, kindness, loving behavior) and strengthened by your attempts to improve, appreciate, connect, and protect.

The foundation of a powerful love relationship lies not in exerting power but in creating value through interest, compassion, and care. That is the only way to change negative impressions partners have of each other.

The self-empowerment that comes from creating value through interest, compassion, and care is its own reward, yet it comes with a significant bonus. The more value we create in love, the more cooperation and mutuality of giving we're likely to experience.
